title: The Fall and the First Promise
summary: Deceived by the serpent, the first couple distrust and disobey God, meet shame and death, yet receive the promise of a Redeemer and God’s covering.
historicalContext: The chapter is set in Eden, the garden the LORD planted for the first pair, where the tree of life grew in the midst beside the one tree God had forbidden. Moses wrote for an Israel that knew serpents as real dangers of the wilderness and as potent symbols in Egyptian and Canaanite religion, where they stood for royal protection, fertility, renewal, or chaos. Genesis refuses every mythic version of the story: the serpent is a creature the LORD God had made, evil enters through a creature’s rebellion and a human choice, and the Creator remains the unchallenged Judge. Israel also knew the sanctuary, and the narrative is full of its vocabulary: God “walking” among His people, an entrance on the east, cherubim guarding the way to His presence, and garments by which God clothes those who come near. Other ancient peoples kept scattered memories of a lost life and a forbidden thing, but none traces human misery so clearly to distrust of a good God’s word, or its remedy so clearly to God Himself.
literaryContext: Genesis 2 closes with a man and woman naked and unashamed; Genesis 3 opens with a serpent described by a near-identical Hebrew word, and the sound-play signals that their openness is about to be exploited. The chapter is carefully ordered. The temptation moves from serpent to woman to man; God’s questions run in reverse, from man to woman to serpent; the sentences return in the first order, serpent, woman, man. At the centre stands the promise of enmity and of the woman’s Seed (3:14-15), so that hope is placed at the heart of the judgment scene. Key words from chapter 2 return with altered meaning: eat, eyes, know, naked, ground, dust, take, and give. The chapter begins the movement of sin and grace that runs through Genesis: Cain’s murder follows at once, the line of the promised seed is traced through Seth, Noah, and Abraham, and the promise of an offspring who blesses the nations grows out of this first word of hope.
themes: The serpent’s lie and the trustworthiness of God’s word
Sin as distrust that ripens into disobedience
Shame, fear, and the breaking of every relationship
Death as the real wages of sin
The first gospel promise of the woman’s Seed
Grace that covers before it sends out

outline.title: The Temptation and the Fall
outline.summary: The serpent casts doubt on God’s word and motives, the woman and then the man eat, and their opened eyes see only shame.

outline.title: The LORD Seeks and Questions
outline.summary: God comes to the garden as before, calls the hiding pair, and draws out a confession tangled with excuses and blame.

outline.title: The Serpent Judged and the Seed Promised
outline.summary: The serpent is cursed and humbled, and God announces lasting enmity and a Seed of the woman who will crush the serpent’s head.

outline.title: Sorrow, Toil, and the Return to Dust
outline.summary: The woman meets pain in childbearing and strain in marriage, the ground is cursed for the man’s sake, and death is declared certain.

outline.title: A Name of Hope, a Covering, and Exile
outline.summary: Adam names Eve in faith, God clothes the pair with skins, and in mercy bars the way to the tree of life.

verses.bibleText: Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Chapter 2 closed with the man and his wife “both naked … and were not ashamed.” Chapter 3 opens with a new figure, and the Hebrew places “the serpent” first for emphasis. The narrator ties the two scenes together with a play of sound: the couple were ʿarummim, naked, and the serpent was ʿarum, “subtil.” Their openness and trust stand beside a creature whose shrewdness is about to be turned against them. The serpent is also called a “beast of the field which the LORD God had made.” It belongs to the created order and possesses no power independent of the Creator. Genesis never allows evil to be a rival god; it appears as a creature turned to wrong use.

The rest of Scripture identifies the one who spoke through the animal. Jesus calls the devil a murderer “from the beginning” and the father of lies (John 8:44). Paul warns that the serpent beguiled Eve “through his subtilty” (2 Corinthians 11:3), and Revelation names “that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan” (Revelation 12:9). A fallen angel used a real creature as his medium. He did not come to the woman in his own form or in the likeness of God, but through a creature placed under human dominion (Genesis 1:28). The test was fair, and nothing compelled her to listen.

The tempter’s first words are a question: “Yea, hath God said …?” The Hebrew can mean “Has God really said that you may not eat of every tree?” or “You shall not eat of any tree,” and the ambiguity serves his purpose. He takes the generous permission of Genesis 2:16, “of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat,” and turns it into a prohibition. God’s abundant provision is made to look like meanness, and the single boundary is enlarged until it seems to define Him.

This is the pattern of temptation throughout Scripture: first doubt what God said, then doubt why He said it. When Jesus met the same enemy in the wilderness, He refused to discuss God’s word as an open question and answered, “It is written” (Matthew 4:4).

wordNotes.term: עָרוּם (ʿarum) — subtil
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective describes shrewdness that can be used well or badly. In Proverbs it is the prudence of the wise who foresee danger; in Job it describes schemers whose plans God frustrates. Here the word is chosen to echo עֲרוּמִּים (ʿarummim), “naked,” in Genesis 2:25. The pair who had nothing to hide meet a creature whose cleverness is bent toward deception.

wordNotes.term: אַף כִּי־אָמַר אֱלֹהִים (ʾaf ki-ʾamar ʾElohim) — Yea, hath God said
wordNotes.explanation: The opening particles express surprise or incredulity, roughly “Is it really so that God said…?” The question presents itself as curiosity while implying that such a command would be unreasonable. The tempter speaks only of Elohim, setting aside the covenant name the narrator uses, and so frames God as remote rather than personal.

verses.bibleText: And the woman said unto the serpent, We may eat of the fruit of the trees of the garden:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the woman said unto the serpent.” Her error begins before her words are examined. She enters a conversation in which God’s goodness is placed on trial, and she does so alone. Until now the only dialogue in the garden has been between God and the man; now a serpent and the woman speak, and the Creator is discussed in His absence. Had she turned from the voice and sought her husband and her Maker, the story would have taken another course.

Her answer begins correctly: “We may eat of the fruit of the trees of the garden.” She defends God against the serpent’s distortion, insisting that the garden is open to them. Yet her reply is slightly weaker than the word she had received. God had said “of every tree” they might “freely eat” (Genesis 2:16), using an emphatic Hebrew construction. In her version the generosity is reduced to a bare permission. The difference is small, but it shows a mind already beginning to see God through the serpent’s frame. Privileges are understated just as the restriction is about to be overstated.

The lesson is practical. Temptation rarely asks for an immediate act of rebellion. It invites a conversation about God, conducted on the tempter’s terms, in which His gifts fade from view. Eve’s response shows how quickly gratitude can shrink when attention fixes on what is withheld. Paul’s concern for the Corinthian church was precisely that their minds might be led astray from “the simplicity that is in Christ,” as Eve’s was (2 Corinthians 11:3). James likewise calls believers to resist the devil and draw near to God rather than to linger in conversation with the enemy (James 4:7-8).

wordNotes.term: מִפְּרִי עֵץ־הַגָּן נֹאכֵל (mipperi ʿets-haggan noʾkhel) — We may eat of the fruit of the trees of the garden
wordNotes.explanation: The woman’s statement is accurate as far as it goes, but it lacks both the word “every” and the emphatic doubling of the verb found in Genesis 2:16 (ʾakhol toʾkhel, “freely eat”). The omission softens the lavishness of God’s gift. Scripture repeatedly ties faithfulness to remembering the fullness of what God has given.

verses.bibleText: But of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden, God hath said, Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Eve now describes the forbidden tree, and three features of her words reveal the drift of her thinking. First, she does not name it. God had called it “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Genesis 2:17); she calls it only “the tree which is in the midst of the garden.” The tree of life also stood in the midst (Genesis 2:9), so her phrasing blurs the distinction between them and treats the forbidden tree as simply one location among others.

Second, she adds to the command: “neither shall ye touch it.” God had forbidden eating, not touching. Some read her addition as a sensible fence around the law, but in context it more likely shows the prohibition growing harsher in her mind. Once God’s restriction is thought of as excessive, it is easily remembered as stricter than He made it. Later Scripture warns against both adding to and subtracting from God’s word (Deuteronomy 4:2; Proverbs 30:6). Doubt can do either.

Third, she softens the penalty. God had said, “in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die” (Genesis 2:17), a construction of certainty. Eve says “lest ye die,” which turns a sure consequence into a possibility. The certainty of the threat has weakened even as the strictness of the command has increased. God has become in her eyes both more demanding and less serious, a combination that makes disobedience feel both justified and safe.

The verse shows how the knowledge of God’s will can remain while trust in His character drains away. Eve still knows there is a command, still knows it concerns death. What she has begun to lose is confidence that the One who spoke it is good. Jesus taught that a person lives “by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4), unaltered and received in trust.

wordNotes.term: פֶּן־תְּמֻתוּן (pen-temutun) — lest ye die
wordNotes.explanation: The particle pen introduces something to be avoided, “so that you do not die.” It is far weaker than God’s own wording in Genesis 2:17, mot tamut, “dying you shall die,” an idiom that stresses certainty. In the woman’s mouth the sentence of death becomes a risk rather than a sure outcome.

wordNotes.term: וְלֹא תִגְּעוּ בּוֹ (velo tiggeʿu bo) — neither shall ye touch it
wordNotes.explanation: The verb nagaʿ means to touch or reach. God’s command concerned eating only. The addition shows the prohibition swelling in Eve’s recollection, making God appear more restrictive than He was, and anticipating the warning that His word must neither be enlarged nor diminished.

verses.bibleText: And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The serpent now drops the posture of an inquirer and contradicts God outright: “Ye shall not surely die.” In Hebrew he takes God’s own phrase from Genesis 2:17, mot tamut, “dying you shall die,” and places the negative before it, so that the denial echoes the exact form of the warning. The effect is to cancel the divine word with its own vocabulary. Eve had weakened the threat to “lest ye die”; the tempter now removes it completely.

This is the first lie recorded in Scripture, and Jesus traces all lying to this source when He calls the devil “a liar, and the father of it” (John 8:44). The lie is aimed directly at the reliability of God. If He had said death would follow and it did not, then His word could not be trusted, His command could be set aside, and His motives would be open to suspicion.

The claim also became the seed of a long religious error. God had warned that sin brings death, the end of the life He had given to the whole person formed from dust (Genesis 2:7). The serpent insisted that humans would not die even if they disobeyed. In many forms that teaching has persisted: that human beings possess a natural immortality, that the soul cannot die, that death is merely a passage into a higher state. Scripture answers that God “only hath immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16), that “the soul that sinneth, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4), and that eternal life is “the gift of God … through Jesus Christ” (Romans 6:23). Life without end is received through Christ and bestowed at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:53-54). It is not a property sinners already hold apart from Him.

The deception was persuasive partly because death did not come at once in its full form. Eve ate and still breathed. Yet from that day the process of dying began, as the rest of the chapter shows. God’s word proved true, and the serpent’s promise of a deathless sin proved false.

wordNotes.term: לֹא־מוֹת תְּמֻתוּן (loʾ-mot temutun) — Ye shall not surely die
wordNotes.explanation: The serpent repeats the emphatic infinitive construction God used in Genesis 2:17 (mot tamut) and sets the negative particle in front of it. The unusual word order makes the negation sweeping: “You will certainly not die.” It is a deliberate and direct contradiction of the Creator’s warning, and it denies that sin carries the penalty of death.

verses.bibleText: For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having denied the penalty, the serpent supplies a motive for the command. “For God doth know” presents the tempter as one with inside knowledge of the divine mind. God, he implies, forbade the tree because He feared rivals. The prohibition was a means of keeping the man and woman small. In a few words the Creator who had given them a world becomes a jealous ruler guarding His privileges.

The promise mixes truth and falsehood with great skill. “In the day ye eat thereof” borrows God’s own phrase from Genesis 2:17. “Your eyes shall be opened” was true in a sense, as verse 7 shows, but the sight gained would be of guilt and nakedness. “Knowing good and evil” was also partly true; they would come to know evil, not by understanding it from above as God does, but by becoming entangled in it. Every element of the promise sounded like enlargement and proved to be loss.

“Ye shall be as gods” is better rendered “as God,” since the word ʾElohim refers to God in the surrounding verses. The serpent offers what he himself had grasped at: equality with the Most High (Isaiah 14:13-14). The heart of the temptation is the desire to define good and evil for oneself, to become the judge of what is right rather than the creature who receives right from the Creator. This is the essence of every later sin.

Paul sets the contrast in Christ. The first Adam reached for equality with God and fell; Christ, who was in the form of God, “thought it not robbery to be equal with God,” yet emptied Himself and became obedient unto death (Philippians 2:6-8). The way to true likeness to God runs through humble trust, not grasping autonomy.

wordNotes.term: כֵּאלֹהִים (keʾlohim) — as gods
wordNotes.explanation: The KJV follows older versions in rendering “as gods,” but the same noun refers to God in verses 1, 3, and 5, so “like God” fits the context well. The participle that follows is plural, which may simply agree with the plural form of ʾElohim or may hint at the heavenly beings of verse 22. Either way the offer is a share in divine status by self-assertion.

wordNotes.term: יֹדְעֵי טוֹב וָרָע (yodʿe tov varaʿ) — knowing good and evil
wordNotes.explanation: “Good and evil” in Hebrew often marks the power to discern and decide what is right, as a judge or king does. The serpent offers the right to determine moral boundaries independently of God. What follows shows that humanity gained experience of evil and lost the clear sight that comes from trusting God’s judgment.

verses.bibleText: And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Nothing in the tree had changed. What changed was the eye that looked at it. Once Eve accepted the serpent’s account of God, the forbidden tree took on a new appearance. The narrator lists three attractions: it was “good for food,” it was “pleasant to the eyes,” and it was “a tree to be desired to make one wise.” The first phrase echoes God’s own verdict over creation, “God saw that it was good” (Genesis 1:4, 31). Now the woman sees and pronounces good on her own authority, in direct opposition to God’s word about this very tree. The judge of good and evil has already changed in her heart.

The three attractions correspond closely to what John later calls “the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16). The sin lay in desiring what He had withheld and in trusting a creature’s promise above the Creator’s. The word translated “to be desired” comes from the same verb used in the tenth commandment, “Thou shalt not covet” (Exodus 20:17). Covetousness had taken root before her hand moved.

“She took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.” The words “with her” need not mean that Adam stood silently beside her throughout the temptation; they can express companionship, that she gave to the one who shared her life. What is clear is that Adam ate knowingly. Paul states that “Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression” (1 Timothy 2:14). The man chose to follow his wife rather than his God, and verse 17 will make that the basis of his sentence.

Scripture therefore traces sin and death to Adam’s choice: “by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin” (Romans 5:12). A single act of eating expressed a whole turning of the heart from trust to self-will. Against it Scripture sets another Man, tempted in all points yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), whose obedience undoes what Adam’s disobedience wrought (Romans 5:19).

wordNotes.term: וְנֶחְמָד הָעֵץ לְהַשְׂכִּיל (venechmad haʿets lehaskil) — a tree to be desired to make one wise
wordNotes.explanation: Nechmad comes from chamad, the verb of the tenth commandment, “Thou shalt not covet.” In Genesis 2:9 the same verb describes trees God made desirable; here desire fastens on the one tree He forbade. Lehaskil means to gain insight or practical success. The woman hoped for a wisdom obtained apart from God, the very wisdom Scripture says begins with fearing Him.

verses.bibleText: And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the eyes of them both were opened.” The serpent’s promise is fulfilled with bitter irony. Their eyes did open, but what they saw was their own exposure. The knowledge they gained was the awareness of guilt. In chapter 2 they were naked and unashamed; now they “knew that they were naked,” and the knowledge was unbearable. Nothing about their bodies had changed. Their relationship with God had changed, and with it their sense of safety before one another.

In Scripture nakedness often signifies vulnerability, defeat, and humiliation (Deuteronomy 28:48; Isaiah 47:3). The first couple felt unprotected because they were. The covering of innocence and communion with God that had surrounded them was gone. Their first response was to manage the problem themselves: “they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.” The verb “made” has been used until now of God’s creative work. Humanity now becomes its own provider of covering, attempting to repair by human effort what sin had destroyed.

The fig-leaf aprons were a poor substitute. Broad enough to hide the body from another’s gaze, they could not remove the guilt that made the couple hide from God, as the next verse shows. Scripture consistently exposes the inadequacy of self-made righteousness (Isaiah 64:6). Only God’s provision in verse 21 will answer the need, anticipating the robe of righteousness God gives to those who trust Him (Isaiah 61:10) and the white raiment Christ offers so that “the shame of thy nakedness do not appear” (Revelation 3:18).

wordNotes.term: עֵירֻמִּם (ʿerummim) — naked
wordNotes.explanation: The spelling differs slightly from ʿarummim in Genesis 2:25, and the word is used elsewhere for people stripped, exposed, and defenceless (Deuteronomy 28:48). Before the fall nakedness meant openness without fear; after it, nakedness becomes the sign of being uncovered before God, with no protection against shame.

wordNotes.term: חֲגֹרֹת (chagorot) — aprons
wordNotes.explanation: The noun means a girdle or loin-covering, a belt-like wrap around the waist. It is a minimal covering, fitting the hurried, self-made effort of the couple. The contrast with the full-length “coats” (kotnot) God makes in verse 21 is intentional.

verses.bibleText: And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The LORD came to the garden as He had before. “They heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day.” The verb “walking” is a form used of God’s presence moving among His people in the sanctuary: “I will walk among you, and will be your God” (Leviticus 26:12; compare 2 Samuel 7:6). Eden was the first place of meeting between God and humanity, and the Creator’s visits there had been occasions of fellowship. He did not change His habits because the couple had changed theirs. The God who had been wronged still came.

“In the cool of the day” renders an expression meaning literally “at the wind of the day,” most naturally the breezy evening hour. The quiet of the setting contrasts sharply with the panic of the human pair. The sound that had once been welcome now filled them with dread.

“Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden.” They took cover among the very trees God had planted for their delight, perhaps near the one that had caused their ruin. Their fig leaves had hidden them from each other; nothing could hide them from God, yet they tried. The instinct to flee from God’s presence has marked fallen humanity ever since (Psalm 139:7-12; Jonah 1:3). Guilt turns the place of communion into a place of fear, and only God’s initiative can bring the hiding sinner back into the light (John 3:19-21).

wordNotes.term: מִתְהַלֵּךְ (mithallek) — walking
wordNotes.explanation: This reflexive form of halak, “to walk,” suggests moving about or walking to and fro. It describes God’s presence in the camp and the tabernacle (Deuteronomy 23:14; 2 Samuel 7:6), linking Eden with the later sanctuary as a place where God dwells among His people.

wordNotes.term: לְרוּחַ הַיּוֹם (leruach hayyom) — in the cool of the day
wordNotes.explanation: Ruach means wind, breath, or spirit; here the phrase most likely marks the time of day when a refreshing breeze arose, toward evening in the Near East. Proposals that it describes a storm of judgment read more into the phrase than the calm narrative suggests.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?” The question was not asked for information. God, who sees in secret, knew where the man was hiding. He asked so that Adam would recognise where he was, not only among the trees but in relation to his Maker. The question gave the sinner opportunity to come forward and confess.

God addresses the man first. Adam had received the command directly (Genesis 2:16-17) and bore responsibility for the household. God begins the inquiry with him, not to excuse the woman, but because the one who first heard the law must first give account. The proceedings resemble a just judge’s careful examination: God does not pronounce sentence until He has drawn out the facts from the accused themselves (compare Genesis 4:9-10; 18:21).

Yet the call is more than legal process. It is the first instance of God seeking the lost. Long before Israel learned that the LORD is merciful and gracious, this question showed that He pursues those who flee Him. The same seeking love speaks through the prophets (Isaiah 65:1-2) and becomes flesh in Jesus, who said He came “to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10). Every gospel call echoes this first one in Eden.

wordNotes.term: אַיֶּכָּה (ʾayyekkah) — Where art thou?
wordNotes.explanation: A single Hebrew word, the interrogative “where” with the second-person suffix. Like God’s question to Cain, “Where is Abel thy brother?”, it is asked by One who already knows. Its purpose is to awaken self-awareness and invite confession rather than to gather facts.

verses.bibleText: And he said, I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Adam answers the question, but not the real issue. “I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.” Each clause is true, and together they form an evasion. He speaks of what he heard, what he felt, and what he did, but not of what he had done to cause it. The consequence is offered in place of the transgression.

The man who once delighted in God’s voice now fears it. Fear is the first emotion Scripture attributes to fallen humanity, and it stands in contrast to the perfect love that “casteth out fear” (1 John 4:18). Adam is also more aware of his shame than of his sin. He feels his exposure keenly while saying nothing of his disobedience, a pattern that marks human nature since the fall: people often hate the results of wrongdoing far more than the wrongdoing itself.

The word “naked” is striking, since Adam was wearing his fig-leaf apron. His covering had failed to give him confidence before God. What he felt was the inner exposure of a guilty conscience, which no garment of his own making could hide (Hebrews 4:13).

wordNotes.term: וָאִירָא (vaʾira) — and I was afraid
wordNotes.explanation: The verb yareʾ covers a range from terror to reverent awe. Here it is the dread of a guilty person before his Judge. Scripture later calls God’s people to a reverent fear that draws near in obedience, quite different from the fear that drives the sinner into hiding.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God responds with two further questions. The first, “Who told thee that thou wast naked?”, implies that another voice has been heard in the garden. Adam’s new sense of exposure did not arise from nowhere. Someone or something has introduced a knowledge God had not given. The question gently uncovers the presence of the tempter and the source of the couple’s distress.

The second question goes to the heart of the matter: “Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?” God names the tree by reference to His own command, repeating the language of Genesis 2:17. The issue is placed where it belongs: not first in the fruit, the serpent, or the woman, but in Adam’s relationship to the word God had spoken directly to him. The phrasing reminds him that the command was given personally and clearly.

The question is still framed so that Adam can answer with a simple confession. A plain “Yes” would have opened the way to honesty. God does not ambush the sinner; He gives him every opportunity to acknowledge his sin, as He does throughout Scripture. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). David found that silence wasted him while confession brought forgiveness (Psalm 32:3-5).

wordNotes.term: מִי הִגִּיד לְךָ (mi higgid lekha) — Who told thee
wordNotes.explanation: The verb higgid means to declare or make known, often of a disclosure or revelation. The pronoun “who” points to a personal source. God’s question implies that an outside voice had taught the couple a new way of seeing themselves, one that did not come from Him.

verses.bibleText: And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Adam’s reply reveals how quickly sin corrupts love and truthfulness. “The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.” The facts are correct; the spirit is not. He mentions the woman before himself and God before both, so that responsibility appears to lie elsewhere. The confession “I did eat” comes last and almost incidentally.

The man who had greeted his wife with joy, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23), now speaks of her distantly as “the woman.” He who had chosen to share her transgression rather than be parted from her now places her between himself and judgment. Sin has turned intimacy into accusation. The cold phrase recalls later family betrayals, as when Jacob’s sons presented Joseph’s coat and called him “thy son” (Genesis 37:32), or when the elder brother said “this thy son” of the prodigal (Luke 15:30).

More seriously, Adam’s words reach past the woman to God Himself: “whom thou gavest.” The gift that God had made for his good is now cited as the cause of his fall. The implication is that the Creator shares the blame. James answers that form of thinking directly: God tempts no one, and every good gift comes from above (James 1:13-17).

Blame-shifting is the natural speech of the guilty heart. It protects the self at the cost of others and ultimately accuses God. By contrast the repentant psalmist says, “Against thee, thee only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4), owning his guilt without excuse.

wordNotes.term: אֲשֶׁר נָתַתָּה עִמָּדִי (ʾasher natattah ʿimmadi) — whom thou gavest to be with me
wordNotes.explanation: The verb natan, “to give,” turns God’s gracious provision in Genesis 2:18-22 into an accusation. Adam presents the woman as God’s placement beside him and implicitly shifts responsibility to the Giver. The phrase shows sin distorting gratitude for a gift into grievance against the One who gave it.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD God said unto the woman, What is this that thou hast done? And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God now turns to the woman: “What is this that thou hast done?” The question is shorter and more direct than those addressed to Adam, inviting her to look squarely at her own act. The same words later confront others whose wrongs could not be hidden (Genesis 12:18; 26:10).

The woman answers, “The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.” Like her husband, she points elsewhere before she admits her part. Yet her answer differs from his in one respect. She claims to have been deceived, and Scripture confirms that she was (2 Corinthians 11:3; 1 Timothy 2:14). Adam’s reply carried no such plea; he had acted knowingly. Deception explains her fall without excusing it, for she had God’s word and chose to trust another.

The chain of blame now runs from man to woman to serpent. God asks the serpent no question. The tempter has no excuse to offer and receives no opportunity to defend himself. The trial of the humans ends with each having admitted “I did eat,” and the sentencing begins with the one who began the evil.

wordNotes.term: הִשִּׁיאַנִי (hishshiʾani) — beguiled me
wordNotes.explanation: The verb nashaʾ means to deceive by false assurance, to lead someone to trust in what will fail them (Jeremiah 49:16; Obadiah 1:3). The Greek Old Testament uses ēpatēsen, and Paul echoes it with an intensified form when he warns that the serpent “beguiled Eve through his subtilty.”

verses.bibleText: And the LORD God said unto the serpent, Because thou hast done this, thou art cursed above all cattle, and above every beast of the field; upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The sentences begin where the evil began. “Because thou hast done this” echoes God’s question to the woman, “What is this that thou hast done?”, and fixes responsibility on the tempter. He is not questioned, for there is nothing to inquire into; his guilt is plain and his intent was wholly malicious.

“Thou art cursed above all cattle, and above every beast of the field.” The wording mirrors verse 1 with deliberate irony. The serpent was more subtil “than any beast of the field”; now it is cursed above every beast of the field. The Hebrew words ʿarum, “subtil,” and ʾarur, “cursed,” sound alike, as though the creature’s cunning had turned into its doom. The curse falls in the first place on the animal that lent itself to Satan’s purpose. Creation itself would carry the marks of sin, and the serpent, once among the most striking of creatures, became a lasting picture of degradation.

“Upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life.” The sentence implies that the serpent’s former bearing was different, though Scripture gives no detail. “Eating dust” is a biblical figure for utter humiliation and defeat; enemies “lick the dust” before the victorious king (Psalm 72:9; Micah 7:17). The words declare that the serpent is brought to the lowest place.

Behind the animal, the sentence strikes the real adversary. “All the days of thy life” sets a limit: the curse lasts until the conflict announced in verse 15 reaches its end. The prophets foresee a renewed creation in which “dust shall be the serpent’s meat,” while harm and destruction cease from God’s holy mountain (Isaiah 65:25). Satan’s humiliation begins in Eden and is completed when he is finally destroyed (Revelation 20:10).

wordNotes.term: אָרוּר (ʾarur) — cursed
wordNotes.explanation: The passive participle of ʾarar describes one placed under a ban, removed from blessing and fruitfulness. It is the opposite of God’s blessing on the creatures in Genesis 1:22, 28. In this chapter only the serpent and the ground are declared cursed; the man and the woman receive sentences but are not themselves cursed.

wordNotes.term: וְעָפָר תֹּאכַל (veʿafar toʾkhal) — dust shalt thou eat
wordNotes.explanation: Biblical writers use the image of eating or licking dust for total defeat and abasement (Psalm 72:9; Isaiah 49:23). The same word ʿafar describes the material from which humanity was formed and to which it returns (verse 19), so the serpent’s sentence also links it with the realm of death it brought into the world.

verses.bibleText: And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
This verse stands at the centre of the chapter and at the root of the whole biblical hope. Here the Lord turns from the literal creature to the power that used it. A snake could not carry the weight of these words; they are addressed to the enemy Scripture later calls “that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan” (Revelation 12:9). Before the man or the woman hears a single word of sentence, God announces His plan to defeat their destroyer. Grace speaks before judgment is finished.

“I will put enmity.” The word stands first in Hebrew for emphasis, and God Himself is the subject. Satan had won the woman’s trust; God declares that He will break that alliance and set hostility in its place. The enmity is His gift. Left to themselves, fallen humans would have remained at peace with the deceiver. By divine grace a hatred of evil and a longing for God would be planted in human hearts.

The conflict widens “between thy seed and her seed.” Two lines of descendants are in view: those who share the serpent’s rebellion, whom Jesus called children of the devil (John 8:44; 1 John 3:8-10), and those who belong to God. Genesis immediately traces this division in Cain and Abel, and then follows the line of promise through Seth, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. From this verse the great controversy between Christ and Satan runs through every age of history.

The climax narrows the “seed” to a single champion: “it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” The pronoun is singular and masculine, and the Greek Old Testament rendered it “he.” The conflict between two communities ends in a decisive encounter between one Offspring of the woman and the serpent himself. The Seed receives a wound to the heel; the serpent receives a crushing blow to the head. Both are struck, but only one blow is fatal.

The New Testament identifies this Seed as Jesus Christ, “made of a woman” (Galatians 4:4), the singular Seed of the promise (Galatians 3:16). Through death He destroyed “him that had the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). At the cross the serpent bruised His heel; in that same death and in His resurrection the serpent’s head was crushed. Believers share the victory, for “the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly” (Romans 16:20). The promise will be finished when the deceiver is destroyed and sin is gone forever (Revelation 20:10).

wordNotes.term: אֵיבָה … זַרְעֲךָ … זַרְעָהּ (ʾevah … zarʿakha … zarʿah) — enmity … thy seed … her seed
wordNotes.explanation: ʾEvah denotes lasting hostility, the settled enmity of ancient foes (Ezekiel 35:5). Zeraʿ, “seed,” can mean a single offspring (Genesis 4:25) or a whole line of descendants, and both senses meet here: a corporate struggle between two lines that culminates in one individual. Paul draws attention to the singular seed of the promise as fulfilled in Christ.

wordNotes.term: הוּא יְשׁוּפְךָ רֹאשׁ (hu yeshufkha roʾsh) — it shall bruise thy head
wordNotes.explanation: The pronoun hu is masculine singular and placed first for emphasis, “He shall bruise”; the Greek Old Testament renders it autos, “he,” though “seed” is neuter in Greek. The verb shuf, used for both blows, means to strike or crush. A wound to the head is mortal; a wound to the heel is grievous yet survivable, so the Seed suffers in the act of conquering.

verses.bibleText: Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Unto the woman he said.” The sentence is introduced without the word “cursed,” which is reserved for the serpent and the ground. The woman remains within the scope of the promise just spoken, for the Seed will be hers. Yet her sin brings real consequences to the two relationships at the centre of her life: motherhood and marriage.

“I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception.” The two nouns likely form a single idea, “your pain in conception,” or pain in the whole process of bearing children. Childbearing itself was part of the original blessing (Genesis 1:28). What changes is that new life will come through suffering. Scripture later uses the anguish of childbirth as an image of intense distress and also of the pain that precedes deliverance (Micah 4:10; John 16:21; Romans 8:22). The very process through which the promised Seed would come into the world would bear the marks of the fall.

“Thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.” In creation the woman was made in God’s image alongside the man (Genesis 1:27) and given to him as a help “meet for him,” a partner corresponding to him (Genesis 2:18). Sin introduced discord, and the sentence describes the strained relationship that would follow. The meaning of “desire” is debated. The same pairing of desire and rule appears in Genesis 4:7, where sin’s desire is to master Cain, which suggests a struggle of wills. The woman’s strong attachment to her husband would remain, yet the relationship would now be marked by his rule over her.

This rule is a consequence of the fall and is announced, not prescribed as the Creator’s ideal. The gospel does not use the verse to sanction harshness. In Christ husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it, and to be gentle rather than bitter (Ephesians 5:25; Colossians 3:19), while husband and wife are “heirs together of the grace of life” (1 Peter 3:7). Grace moves the marriage relationship back toward the self-giving partnership God designed in the beginning.

wordNotes.term: עִצְּבוֹנֵךְ (ʿitstsevonekh) — thy sorrow
wordNotes.explanation: ʿItstsavon means pain, toil, or hard labour. It appears only three times in the Old Testament, here, in verse 17 for the man’s toil with the ground, and in Genesis 5:29. The repetition links the woman’s and the man’s sentences: both now meet suffering in the very spheres where God first gave blessing.

wordNotes.term: תְּשׁוּקָתֵךְ (teshuqatekh) — thy desire
wordNotes.explanation: Teshuqah occurs only three times. In Song of Solomon 7:10 it is the lover’s longing; in Genesis 4:7 it is sin’s urge to master Cain, again paired with the verb “rule.” The Greek Old Testament rendered it “turning.” The word denotes a strong pull toward someone, and here it stands beside the husband’s rule to depict a marriage strained by sin.

verses.bibleText: And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And unto Adam he said.” The sentence on the man is the longest, and God first states its ground. “Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife.” The Hebrew phrase “hearken to the voice of” is the regular idiom for obedience, normally used of obeying God. Adam had given to his wife’s word the place that belonged to the Creator’s. God then repeats His command almost word for word, “Thou shalt not eat of it,” reminding Adam that the prohibition had been spoken to him personally (Genesis 2:17).

“Cursed is the ground for thy sake.” Once again the curse does not fall directly on the man. It falls on the ground, the ʾadamah from which ʾadam was formed (Genesis 2:7). Humanity was made to rule the earth as God’s steward; now the earth resists its ruler. Creation suffers because of the sin of the one placed over it, and Paul describes the whole creation as subjected to frustration and groaning while it waits for redemption (Romans 8:20-22).

“In sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life.” The word for “sorrow” is the same one used in verse 16 for the woman’s pain. Work itself was given before the fall (Genesis 2:15); what is new is that labour becomes painful, uncertain, and frequently frustrated. The verb “eat,” so central to the sin, appears repeatedly in God’s words to Adam. He ate what was forbidden; now his eating will come only through hardship. The phrase “all the days of thy life” also signals that his days are numbered.

wordNotes.term: שָׁמַעְתָּ לְקוֹל אִשְׁתֶּךָ (shamaʿta leqol ʾishtekha) — thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife
wordNotes.explanation: Shamaʿ leqol, “to listen to the voice of,” is the common Hebrew idiom for obeying. It is used of heeding the LORD’s voice (Exodus 15:26) and of Saul’s fatal choice to obey the people instead (1 Samuel 15:24). Adam’s sin is described as a transfer of obedience from God to another voice.

wordNotes.term: בַּעֲבוּרֶךָ (baʿavurekha) — for thy sake
wordNotes.explanation: The preposition baʿavur means “on account of” or “because of.” The ground is cursed because of the man’s sin. Its use elsewhere can also carry the sense of “for the benefit of,” and Scripture shows hardship serving God’s corrective purpose, though the primary sense here is causal.

verses.bibleText: Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee.” The ground that once yielded trees “pleasant to the sight, and good for food” (Genesis 2:9) will now also produce growth that hinders and wounds. Labour will be spent not only on cultivation but in fighting the soil’s resistance. The thorn becomes a lasting emblem of the curse (Hebrews 6:8).

“And thou shalt eat the herb of the field.” Adam’s diet had been fruit and seed-bearing plants of the garden (Genesis 1:29; 2:16). Now he would also depend on field plants raised by toil from the ground. The contrast marks a lowering of his condition, from the abundance of Eden to hard-won crops outside it.

Thorns appear again at the climax of redemption. The soldiers pressed a crown of thorns on the head of Jesus (John 19:2). The One who would remove the curse wore its emblem, and the prophets foresee a day when the myrtle replaces the brier (Isaiah 55:13).

wordNotes.term: קוֹץ וְדַרְדַּר (qots vedardar) — thorns and thistles
wordNotes.explanation: Qots is a general word for thorny plants, and dardar denotes thistles or prickly weeds. The pair appears again only in Hosea 10:8, growing over Israel’s ruined altars, an image of desolation. Together they picture land that resists and wounds those who work it.

verses.bibleText: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.” Survival will now require exhausting labour, the kind that leaves the brow wet. Bread, the staple of life, will be wrested from the ground through effort. Even so, work outside Eden remained a means of discipline and grace. Toil restrains idleness, teaches dependence, and keeps fallen people from many temptations (Proverbs 6:6-11; 2 Thessalonians 3:10-12).

“Till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.” The sentence of Genesis 2:17 is here confirmed in plain words. The man was formed “of the dust of the ground” and became a living soul when God breathed into him the breath of life (Genesis 2:7). Death reverses that process. Life does not continue in some other form; the person returns to the dust from which he was taken, and “the spirit,” the breath of life, returns to God who gave it (Ecclesiastes 12:7). The serpent had promised that they would not die; God declares that they will.

This verse refutes the serpent’s lie and every doctrine of innate immortality that grew from it. Human beings are mortal by nature since the fall. Scripture describes the dead as resting in the dust, unconscious, awaiting the voice of God (Psalm 146:4; Daniel 12:2; John 11:11-14). Hope lies not in an immortal soul but in the resurrection, when “many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake” (Daniel 12:2).

The grace in the sentence is the delay. Adam did not die on the day he sinned as the full stroke of judgment; he was given time, a probation in which to receive the promise of verse 15. And the One who would be bruised for him would enter the dust of death Himself and rise from it (Psalm 22:15; 1 Corinthians 15:20-22), so that those who return to dust may one day rise in Him.

wordNotes.term: עָפָר אַתָּה וְאֶל־עָפָר תָּשׁוּב (ʿafar ʾattah veʾel-ʿafar tashuv) — dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return
wordNotes.explanation: ʿAfar is the loose soil from which God formed the man (Genesis 2:7). The sentence states that the human being, as a whole person, is dust animated by God’s breath, and at death returns to that state. The same language describes all creatures returning to dust when God withdraws their breath, with life restored only by His renewed act.

verses.bibleText: And Adam called his wife's name Eve; because she was the mother of all living.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Adam called his wife’s name Eve; because she was the mother of all living.” The verse can seem abruptly placed after the sentence of death, but its position is the point. Adam has just heard that he will return to dust. His response is to give his wife a name meaning “life.” He takes God at His word in both directions: death is certain, and so is the promise that the woman will bear a Seed who will overcome the serpent.

In Genesis 2:23 the man called her “Woman,” recognising her origin from himself. Now he names her by her future. She has not yet borne a child, yet he calls her the mother of all living. This is an act of faith, resting on what God had said in verse 15, and it shows a man turning back toward the Lord after his fall. Hebrews describes faith as “the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1); Adam’s naming of Eve is an early example.

The name looks beyond natural motherhood. Every human being would descend from her, but the hope of the race lay in one particular descendant. Through her line life would triumph over the death her choice had helped to bring, as Paul says: “as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

wordNotes.term: חַוָּה (chavvah) — Eve
wordNotes.explanation: The name is related to the Hebrew verb chayah, “to live,” and the narrator explains it by the phrase that follows. The Greek Old Testament translated it here as Zōē, “Life,” before transliterating it as Heua in Genesis 4:1, from which English “Eve” comes. The name expresses hope spoken in the shadow of the death sentence.

wordNotes.term: אֵם כָּל־חָי (ʾem kol-chay) — the mother of all living
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase identifies Eve as the source of every human life to come. The form “was” in Hebrew anticipates what is certain though not yet seen. Paul’s argument that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men” rests on this common descent.

verses.bibleText: Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.” The verse answers verse 7. There the couple “made themselves” aprons of leaves; here the LORD God makes garments and clothes them. The same verb “made” appears in both places, setting human effort beside divine provision. Their covering was hurried, partial, and fragile. His covering is complete and lasting, and He places it on them Himself.

The garments are “coats,” full tunics, and they are made of “skins.” For skins to be provided, animals had to die. This is the first death recorded in Scripture, and it occurs because of human sin, though the creatures themselves had done no wrong. The text does not describe an altar, yet the sequence strongly suggests that sacrifice began here. In the next chapter Abel brings the firstlings of his flock, and God accepts his offering (Genesis 4:4), which implies that the way of approach through an animal’s death had already been made known. From the beginning, sinners learned that their covering would cost the life of another.

The language of the verse also recalls the sanctuary. The word for “coats” is used for the tunics of Israel’s priests, and the verb “clothed” describes Moses dressing Aaron and his sons for service (Exodus 28:41; Leviticus 8:13). God clothes the fallen pair before He sends them out, preparing them to live and worship in His presence even outside the garden.

The gospel shines through the act. Sinners cannot cover their own guilt. God provides the covering through a substitute’s death, and He puts it on those who cannot clothe themselves. Isaiah rejoices that God “hath clothed me with the garments of salvation” (Isaiah 61:10), and the redeemed are arrayed in white robes washed in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14).

wordNotes.term: כָּתְנוֹת עוֹר (kotnot ʿor) — coats of skins
wordNotes.explanation: Kuttonet is a long tunic, the garment worn by Joseph (Genesis 37:3) and by Israel’s priests (Exodus 28:39-40). ʿOr means skin or hide, so the tunics were made from animal skins. Compared with the small leaf aprons of verse 7, these were full garments, suited to life outside Eden and implying the death of animals.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּלְבִּשֵׁם (vayyalbishem) — and clothed them
wordNotes.explanation: The causative form of labash, “to put on clothing,” means to dress another person. It is the verb used when Moses clothes the priests for their ministry (Exodus 29:8; Leviticus 8:13). God does more than supply garments; He clothes the couple Himself, an act of personal care and gracious provision.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil: and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the LORD God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil.” God speaks as in Genesis 1:26, “Let us make man,” with a plural that reflects the fullness of the Godhead in deliberation. What the serpent promised has come true only in a twisted sense. The man now knows good and evil, but not as God knows it. God knows evil as the Holy One who sees and judges it from above. Humanity now knows it from within, by participation, by guilt, and by its consequences.

The sentence breaks off: “and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever.” The Hebrew leaves the thought unfinished, and verse 23 completes it with action. The tree of life had been freely available (Genesis 2:9, 16). Now it must be withheld. Life without end is not a natural possession of human beings; it was available only by continued access to what God supplied. Cut off from that source, the sinner would die, as God had warned.

The barrier was an act of mercy. For sinners to go on living forever in a state of rebellion, shame, and decay would have made evil permanent. God would not allow sin to be immortalised. The Bible consistently presents immortality as God’s gift to the redeemed, bestowed through Christ at the resurrection (Romans 2:7; 1 Corinthians 15:53-54; 2 Timothy 1:10).

The tree of life reappears at the close of Scripture, standing beside the river in the city of God, with leaves for the healing of the nations. Those who wash their robes will have “right to the tree of life” (Revelation 22:2, 14). What was barred in Genesis is restored through the Lamb.

wordNotes.term: כְּאַחַד מִמֶּנּוּ (keʾachad mimmennu) — as one of us
wordNotes.explanation: The first-person plural recalls “Let us make man” (Genesis 1:26) and “let us go down” (Genesis 11:7). It suits a God whose unity includes plurality, a hint fulfilled in the fuller revelation of Father, Son, and Spirit. The comparison concerns only knowing good and evil, not sharing God’s holiness or life.

wordNotes.term: וָחַי לְעֹלָם (vachay leʿolam) — and live for ever
wordNotes.explanation: Chay means to live, and leʿolam means for a long or unending time. The phrase shows that unending life depended on access to the tree God provided. Without it the sentence of death stands. Scripture never ascribes endless life to human nature as such; God alone has it inherently and grants it as a gift.

verses.bibleText: Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden.” The unfinished thought of verse 22 is completed by action. The verb “sent forth” is the same used when Noah sent forth the raven and the dove; it marks a departure that is decisive. The man is no longer to live in the place God prepared for communion with Him.

Yet his purpose is not taken away. He goes out “to till the ground from whence he was taken.” Before the garden was planted, there was no man to till the ground (Genesis 2:5); inside the garden the man was placed to dress and keep it (Genesis 2:15). Now he will work the same kind of soil outside Eden, under the curse, reminded daily of his origin and his destiny. The ground he works is the ground that formed him and will receive him.

The sentence is severe, but God still gives work, food, and time. Life outside Eden is lived in hope of return, a hope that runs through Israel’s exiles and homecomings to the promise of a restored earth where God dwells with His people (Revelation 21:3).

wordNotes.term: לַעֲבֹד אֶת־הָאֲדָמָה (laʿavod ʾet-haʾadamah) — to till the ground
wordNotes.explanation: ʿAvad means to work, serve, or cultivate, and is used both for labour on the land and for service in worship. The phrase deliberately echoes Genesis 2:5 and 2:15. The calling to work the ground continues after the fall, but now the ʾadamah resists the man formed from it.

verses.bibleText: So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“So he drove out the man.” The verb is stronger than “sent forth” in verse 23. It is used later of God driving out the nations before Israel and of Cain’s banishment (Genesis 4:14; Exodus 23:30). The repetition stresses that the expulsion was not voluntary and could not be reversed by human effort.

“And he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.” The entrance to the garden was on the east, as the entrance to the tabernacle and the temple would later face east. Cherubim appear throughout Scripture as heavenly beings close to God’s throne. Their figures were embroidered on the tabernacle curtains and fashioned over the mercy seat in the most holy place (Exodus 25:18-22; 26:31). Eden was the first sanctuary, and the same guardians that later marked God’s holy presence now barred the way to the tree of life. The “flaming sword” is literally “the flame of the sword which turned itself,” flashing light moving in every direction. Light and fire often accompany the divine presence in Scripture (Exodus 3:2; Ezekiel 1:13), and the gate may have remained a place where the faithful came to worship near the glory they could no longer enter.

The verb “to keep” is the same one used for the man’s task of keeping the garden (Genesis 2:15). The steward who failed to guard it is replaced by heavenly guardians who keep the way shut.

The chapter ends with the way closed, but Scripture does not leave it so. Through the veil of His flesh Christ has opened “a new and living way” into God’s presence (Hebrews 10:19-20). He is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). In the new creation the tree of life stands open again, and the redeemed eat of it in the paradise of God (Revelation 2:7).

wordNotes.term: הַכְּרֻבִים (hakkeruvim) — Cherubims
wordNotes.explanation: Keruvim is already a Hebrew plural, so the KJV’s “Cherubims” doubles the plural ending. Cherubim are heavenly beings associated with God’s throne and holiness; they bear His presence and guard what is sacred. Their figures overshadowed the ark and adorned the sanctuary, linking Eden’s gate with Israel’s place of worship.

wordNotes.term: לַהַט הַחֶרֶב הַמִּתְהַפֶּכֶת (lahat hacherev hammithappekhet) — a flaming sword which turned every way
wordNotes.explanation: Lahat means flame or blaze, so the phrase is literally “the flame of the sword.” The reflexive participle mithappekhet describes something turning itself back and forth, a continual flashing movement. The image is of living, dazzling brightness that no one could pass, a sign of God’s holy presence guarding the way.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: Why does the first temptation begin with a question about what God said rather than with an open invitation to rebel?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Sin entered when the first couple trusted the serpent’s word above God’s, bringing shame, alienation, and death; yet God answered at once with the promise of a Seed who would crush the serpent and with a covering only He could provide.
discussionQuestions: How does the serpent move from a question, to a denial, to an accusation against God’s character?
What do the fig leaves and the hiding among the trees reveal about the first human response to guilt?
Why is it significant that the promise of the Seed comes before the sentences on the woman and the man?
In what sense is the barring of the tree of life an act of mercy as well as judgment?
How does Genesis 3 explain both the dignity and the mortality of human beings?
commonMisunderstandings: The serpent’s claim that death would not follow is not a harmless myth; it is the first lie, and it lies at the root of the idea that human beings are naturally immortal.
The fall was not a step upward into maturity; the knowledge gained was the experience of guilt and loss.
God did not curse the man or the woman; the curse falls on the serpent and the ground, while the couple receive sentences shaped by mercy.
The rule of the husband in 3:16 describes a consequence of sin rather than the Creator’s ideal of partnership, and it never licenses harshness.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the order of the chapter in view: distrust of God’s word comes before the act of eating, and God’s promise of redemption comes before the sentences are spoken. Present the serpent as Satan’s instrument, death as real, and Christ as the Seed who conquers by being wounded.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: The God who called “Where art thou?” still seeks those who hide. Rather than sewing our own coverings, we may come out from among the trees, confess what we have done, and receive the covering He provides through the Seed who bore the serpent’s strike for us.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Sin and death entered through distrust of God’s word, and God immediately promised a Redeemer, the woman’s Seed, who would defeat Satan through His own suffering.
flow: God gave every good thing and one clear command to test loving trust.
Satan, speaking through the serpent, denied that sin brings death and slandered God’s motives.
Disobedience brought shame, fear, broken relationships, and the certainty of returning to dust.
God sought the sinners, promised a Seed to crush the serpent, and clothed them through the death of another.
Jesus is that Seed; through His death and resurrection He offers life to all who trust Him.
simpleIllustrations: A child who breaks something precious may hide behind the furniture, but the parent who calls out is coming to restore, not merely to punish.
A homemade bandage of leaves cannot close a deep wound; healing requires the physician’s own work.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you stop hiding behind your own coverings and accept the covering God provides in Jesus, the promised Seed?
cautions: Do not blame the woman for the fall in a way that excuses the man, whom Scripture holds responsible for sin entering the world.
Do not treat the serpent as a mere symbol detached from the personal enemy Scripture names Satan.
Do not suggest that the soul escapes death; the sentence is a return to dust, and life beyond it comes by resurrection.

reflectionQuestions: Where am I tempted to question what God has clearly said because I want what He has withheld?
What fig leaves have I sewn to manage my guilt instead of bringing it honestly to God?
When God asks me “Where art thou?”, do I answer with confession or with blame?
How does the promise of the wounded yet victorious Seed change the way I face my own failures?
What would it mean for me to receive God’s covering rather than trust my own?
